concepts.name: Constitutional vs. Statutory Status of CVC
key_dimensions: CVC is NOT a constitutional body — established by CVC Act, 2003 (common UPSC trap)
Origins in executive resolution (1964, on Santhanam Committee recommendations) vs. statutory recognition
Comparison with constitutional vigilance bodies like CAG or UPSC
Vineet Narain case (1997) Supreme Court directions that preceded statutory status

concepts.name: Composition and Appointment of CVC
key_dimensions: Central Vigilance Commissioner (chairperson) + up to 2 Vigilance Commissioners
Appointment by President on recommendation of a 3-member committee: PM, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha
Eligibility: persons of impeccable integrity from specified service backgrounds
Distinction between appointment procedure of CVC vs. CBI Director (different committee compositions — UPSC trap)

concepts.name: Tenure, Removal, and Service Conditions of CVC Members
key_dimensions: 4-year term OR until age 65, whichever is earlier
Removal only by Presidential order after Supreme Court inquiry — mirrors Election Commissioner removal (important comparison)
Not eligible for further employment under Central or State government after retirement
Salaries/allowances charged to Consolidated Fund of India — ensuring financial independence

concepts.name: Jurisdiction of CVC: Who Falls Under Its Purview
key_dimensions: Covers Central Government employees, PSU officers, nationalized banks, Central cooperative institutions
Specific focus on Group A officers and above; does NOT cover state government employees (key limitation)
Jurisdiction over CBI for superintendence in corruption cases under PC Act only — NOT general superintendence
Exclusion of armed forces from CVC jurisdiction — common trap

concepts.name: CVC's Superintendence Over CBI: Scope and Limits
key_dimensions: CVC superintendence over CBI limited to Prevention of Corruption Act cases only
General superintendence of CBI vests with Ministry of Personnel — a critical distinction
Vineet Narain case mandated CVC superintendence to insulate CBI from political interference
CVC cannot direct CBI on investigation of specific cases or interfere in operational decisions

concepts.name: CVC's Role vs. CBI's Role: Functional Overlap and Distinction
key_dimensions: CVC is advisory/recommendatory; CBI is an investigative agency — different nature of functions
CVC can call for investigation reports from CBI but cannot direct investigation outcomes
CVC reviews CBI's work in PC Act cases; CBI submits quarterly reports to CVC
CVC can recommend prosecution but final decision rests with the competent authority

concepts.name: Advisory and Recommendatory Nature of CVC
key_dimensions: CVC recommendations are NOT binding on the government — most critical limitation
Ministries/departments must consult CVC in cases of corruption but may disagree with reasons
CVC can only 'recommend' penalty; disciplinary authority retains final power
Comparison with CBI where prosecution sanction is mandatory — distinguishing advisory vs. mandatory functions

concepts.name: Chief Vigilance Officers (CVOs): Appointment and Dual Role
key_dimensions: CVOs appointed in each Ministry/PSU to act as extended arm of CVC
CVO has a dual reporting structure: administrative head of organization AND CVC
CVC consults on the appointment and transfer of CVOs — ensures independence
CVO handles departmental inquiries and vigilance work at the organizational level

concepts.name: CVC and Whistleblower Protection: PIDPI Resolution
key_dimensions: CVC designated as the nodal agency under Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informers (PIDPI) Resolution, 2004
CVC can receive complaints about corruption against government servants while protecting identity
Distinction between PIDPI (executive resolution) and Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (statutory — different authority)
CVC's role in directing CBI/police to investigate complaints received under PIDPI

concepts.name: CVC's Power to Investigate Complaints: Process and Limitations
key_dimensions: CVC can either inquire itself OR refer the matter to CBI or Chief Vigilance Officer
No power of direct prosecution; cannot register FIRs unlike CBI
Complaints against officers of the level of Joint Secretary and above referred to CVC mandatorily
Single Directive controversy: CVC's instruction requiring prior approval before investigating Joint Secretary+ officials

concepts.name: Annual Report of CVC: Significance and Addressee
key_dimensions: CVC submits annual report to the President (NOT Parliament directly)
President causes the report to be laid before each House of Parliament
Report covers nature and extent of corruption, action taken, systemic improvements suggested
Comparison: CAG reports directly to President; CVC also reports to President — but CAG has constitutional status

concepts.name: Santhanam Committee (1964): Origins and Recommendations
key_dimensions: Committee on Prevention of Corruption headed by K. Santhanam recommended creation of CVC
Recommended an independent watchdog insulated from executive interference
Original CVC was an executive body (1964 resolution); statutory status came only in 2003
Committee also recommended strengthening of vigilance machinery at departmental levels — origins of CVO system

concepts.name: Vineet Narain vs. Union of India (1997): Judicial Directions and Impact
key_dimensions: Hawala scandal case; SC directed that CBI shall not be under political control in PC Act cases
SC mandated CVC superintendence over CBI for PC Act investigations
Court directed that the Single Directive (protecting senior officials) was unconstitutional in its earlier avatar
Case directly led to CVC Act, 2003 — landmark example of judicial legislation on vigilance

concepts.name: CVC vs. Lokpal: Jurisdictional Boundaries and Overlap
key_dimensions: Lokpal Act, 2013 covers PM, Ministers, MPs, Group A officers; CVC covers Group A and below in departments
Lokpal can refer cases to CBI; CVC also refers cases to CBI — potential overlap in Group A officer cases
Lokpal has powers of prosecution sanction for Group A officers; CVC is only recommendatory
CVC functions as a supplementary body; Lokpal does NOT subsume CVC — both coexist (UPSC trap)

concepts.name: CVC vs. State Vigilance Commissions and Lokayuktas
key_dimensions: CVC jurisdiction is exclusively Central — no authority over state government employees
States have their own Lokayuktas/State Vigilance Commissions (not mandated by CVC Act)
Lokpal Act mandates states to establish Lokayuktas within 1 year — but no uniformity in structure
Absence of a central supervisory body over state anti-corruption machinery — systemic gap

concepts.name: Single Directive Controversy: Protection of Senior Officials
key_dimensions: Single Directive required prior approval of competent authority before CBI investigates Joint Secretary+ officials
SC struck down Single Directive in Vineet Narain case as violating equality before law
Government reintroduced similar protection through Section 6A of DSPE Act — later struck down by SC in 2014 (Subramanian Swamy case)
Ongoing tension between protecting honest officers and enabling investigation of powerful officials

concepts.name: CVC's Role in Systemic Improvement and Preventive Vigilance
key_dimensions: CVC not just punitive — mandated to suggest systemic improvements to minimize corruption opportunities
Issues circulars and guidelines on procurement, tendering, financial management to departments
Distinction between punitive vigilance (action after corruption) vs. preventive vigilance (system reforms)
CVC's Integrity Index and e-governance promotion as modern preventive vigilance tools

concepts.name: Limitations and Criticisms of CVC
key_dimensions: No binding powers — recommendations routinely ignored by ministries (fundamental structural weakness)
Cannot investigate state-level corruption or private sector corruption
Understaffed relative to mandate; depends on CVOs who have conflicts of interest
No witness protection or special courts under CVC Act — prosecution remains slow under regular courts

concepts.name: CVC Act, 2003: Key Provisions and Scope
key_dimensions: Gave statutory basis to CVC; also placed CBI's superintendence in PC Act cases with CVC in statutory form
Defined 'scheduled offences' (mainly under Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988) over which CVC has oversight
Act specifies that CVC shall consist of CVC + not more than 2 Vigilance Commissioners
Comparison: DSPE Act governs CBI's establishment; CVC Act governs CVC — two separate statutes (UPSC trap)

concepts.name: Relationship Between CVC and Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT)
key_dimensions: DoPT is the administrative ministry for CBI; CVC has vigilance superintendence — dual accountability structure
Transfer and posting of CBI Director involves CVC, DoPT, and high-powered committee
Policy on disciplinary proceedings for Central services routed through DoPT; CVC provides vigilance angle
Tension between DoPT's administrative control and CVC's functional independence over anti-corruption work
